# Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026: permitting reform tracker

> Section index, plain-language summaries, verbatim quotes with page and line cites, and a comparison with the SPEED Act and the Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024. Bill text released 2026-09-30; 417 pages, 71 sections. Data as of 2026-10-02.

## Reading and retrieval

Independent tracker. BAAJA is the September 30, 2026 draft, not enacted law. Summaries are AI-assisted. Verify legal claims against the official PDF and compare the specified versions, not later amendments.
PDF citations use printed bill pages and lines. A matching quote proves occurrence; it does not validate nearby interpretations. Source positions describe the cited item, not every position held by its author.
- [No-JavaScript section index](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/reading.html)
- [Full text and analysis](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/llms-full.txt): all sections, comparisons, timeline, people and media with citations.
- [Tracker JSON](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/data/core.json): the same data the browser renders, including check coverage.
- [Bill paragraph JSON](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/data/bill.json): section number to [printed page, line, indent level, text] arrays.
- Fetch sections/{number}.md for one section. Each file includes its summary, cited key points, quotes, comparison notes and full statutory text.
- Browser search: #/bill/search/{URL-encoded query}; section: #/bill/sec/{number}; passage: #/bill/sec/{number}/{page}-{line}. Fragment routes require JavaScript; use the Markdown or JSON endpoints for HTTP retrieval.

# Sec. 1101. Purposes; procedure; savings provision

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1101)

## Summary

Rewrites NEPA's opening section. Adds a statement that NEPA prescribes a procedure for considering and informing the public about the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of major federal actions, producing an informational document, and a savings clause that NEPA mandates no particular outcome.

## Key points

- Codifies NEPA as a procedural statute whose product is an informational document ([p. 5, line 14 to p. 5, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=5))
- New savings provision: nothing in NEPA mandates a particular outcome ([p. 5, line 17 to p. 5, line 19](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=5))

## Selected statutory quotes

> Nothing in this Act mandates a particular outcome as a result of the use of the procedure described in subsection (b).

[p. 5, line 17 to p. 5, line 19](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=5)

States in the statute that NEPA is procedural, as the Supreme Court held in Seven County.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

Current NEPA section 2 states purposes only; the procedure and savings language is new.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 did not amend NEPA's purposes section.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(a)) added a subsection to NEPA section 2 calling the law 'a purely procedural statute' that 'does not mandate particular results'. The Senate text says the same thing in different words.

# Sec. 1102. Definitions

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1102)

## Summary

Moves NEPA's definitions from section 111 to a new section 3 and expands them. New terms include agency chief environmental review and permitting officers, eNEPA technologies, key permitting agencies, a 20-page record of stakeholder engagement, record of decision, and statement of purpose and need.

The bill lists 14 kinds of action that are not major federal actions and so fall outside NEPA. A project whose only federal involvement is a loan or loan guarantee is out. So are routine administrative actions under $10 million, and repair or replacement of lifeline infrastructure that adds no more than 20 percent capacity.

The list also excludes geothermal observation test projects, transmission upgrades under new Federal Power Act section 216A(b), covered Natural Gas Act pipeline work, actions another agency already evaluated, and Army Corps continuing-authority or environmental-infrastructure projects with a federal share of $50 million or less.

## Key points

- Loans and loan guarantees alone no longer make a project a major federal action ([p. 17, line 1 to p. 17, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=17))
- Lifeline infrastructure repair and replacement excluded if capacity grows by 20 percent or less and no new through lanes ([p. 19, line 8 to p. 19, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=19))
- Corps continuing-authority and environmental infrastructure projects excluded up to a $50 million federal share ([p. 21, line 1 to p. 21, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=21))
- New 'key permitting agency' list: USDA, Commerce, Interior, Energy, Transportation, Defense, EPA, FERC, NRC, DHS, HUD, the Corps, ACHP ([p. 15, line 7 to p. 15, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=15))
- Defines a 20-page record of stakeholder engagement documenting pre-application outreach ([p. 21, line 23 to p. 21, line 25](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=21))

## Selected statutory quotes

> for which the only Federal involvement is a loan guarantee or loan;

[p. 17, line 1 to p. 17, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=17)

A loan or loan guarantee alone no longer brings a project under NEPA.

> any proposed agency action associated with a project to repair, reconstruct, restore, retrofit, or replace lifeline infrastructure

[p. 18, line 22 to p. 18, line 25](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=18)

Repair and replacement of existing roads, bridges, pipes and lines are excluded.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

NEPA section 111 (added by the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023) lists seven exclusions: non-federal actions with no or minimal federal funding or involvement, general revenue sharing, loans and loan guarantees where the agency lacks sufficient control over their use, SBA loan guarantees, enforcement actions, extraterritorial actions, and non-discretionary actions.

The bill makes a loan or loan guarantee an exclusion on its own terms when it is the only federal involvement. It covers grants and cost-share awards where the agency lacks predominant control. It adds seven exclusions: routine administrative actions up to $10 million, lifeline infrastructure repair, geothermal test projects, in-corridor transmission work, in-corridor gas pipeline work, actions another agency already reviewed, and Corps projects with a federal share up to $50 million.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 did not amend NEPA definitions.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(f)) added grants and cost-share awards to the financial-assistance exclusion, required 'complete' agency control before funding counts, excluded Farm Service Agency loans and actions already reviewed by another agency, and said federal funding alone cannot make an action major. It also defined 'reasonably foreseeable' effects as those with a close causal relationship to the project. The Senate bill has no such definition in NEPA and no limit on the scope of effects an agency may study; its list of excluded actions is longer.

“(1) AGENCY CERPO.—The term ‘agency CERPO’ means the chief environmental review and permitting officer of each key permitting agency, as appointed by the head of the key permitting agency.

[p. 6, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=6) (indent level 2)

“(2) AUTHORIZATION.—The term ‘authorization’ means any lease, right-of-way, easement, license, permit, approval, finding, determination, or other administrative decision issued by a Federal agency or any interagency consultation that is required or authorized under Federal law to implement a proposed agency action.

[p. 6, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=6) (indent level 2)

“(3) CATEGORICAL EXCLUSION.—The term ‘categorical exclusion’ means a category of actions that a Federal agency has determined, or Congress has deemed by statute, normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment, within the meaning of section 102(2)(C).

[p. 6, line 18](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=6) (indent level 2)

“(4) CHAIRMAN.—The term ‘Chairman’ means the Chairman of the Council.

[p. 6, line 20](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=6) (indent level 2)

“(5) COOPERATING AGENCY.—The term ‘cooperating agency’ means any Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency (including a county, borough, parish, city, and any other political subdivision of a State) that has been designated as a cooperating agency under section 107(a)(2)(A).

[p. 7, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=7) (indent level 2)

“(6) COUNCIL.—The term ‘Council’ means the Council on Environmental Quality established by section 202.

“(7) ENEPA TECHNOLOGIES.—The term ‘eNEPA technologies’ means digital tools, applications, and other technological capabilities used by agencies to support the responsibilities of the agency with respect to environmental review or other types of authorizations.

[p. 7, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=7) (indent level 2)

“(8) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—The term ‘environmental assessment’ means an environmental assessment prepared under section 106(b)(1)(A).

“(10) ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT.— The term ‘environmental impact statement’ means a detailed written statement that is required by section 102(2)(C).

“(18) MAJOR FEDERAL ACTION.—

[p. 16, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=16) (indent level 3)

“(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘major Federal action’ means a proposed agency action subject to the requirements of this Act that the agency carrying out the proposed agency action determines is subject to substantial Federal control and responsibility.

“(B) EXCLUSIONS.—The term ‘major Federal action’ does not include—

[p. 17, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=17) (indent level 5)

“(III) for which the only Federal involvement is a loan guarantee or loan;

“(ii) funding assistance solely in the form of general revenue-sharing funds which do not provide Federal agency compliance or enforcement responsibility over the subsequent use of such funds;

“(iv) business loan guarantees provided by the Small Business Administration pursuant to subsection (a) or (b) of section 7 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 636) or title V of the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 (15 U.S.C. 695 et seq.);

[p. 17, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=17) (indent level 4)

“(v) bringing judicial or administrative civil or criminal enforcement actions;

“(vii) activities or decisions that are non-discretionary and made in accordance with the statutory authority of the agency;

[p. 18, line 21](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=18) (indent level 4)

“(ix) notwithstanding any other provision of law, any proposed agency action associated with a project to repair, reconstruct, restore, retrofit, or replace lifeline infrastructure (as defined in section 4 of the Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act of 1977 (42 U.S.C. 7703) and referred to in this clause as ‘lifeline infrastructure’), if the head of the relevant Federal agency determines the repair, reconstruction, restoration, retrofit, or replacement is in the immediate vicinity of the lifeline infrastructure and does not alter the function or increase the capacity of the lifeline infrastructure by more than 20 percent as compared to the capacity of the original condition of the lifeline infrastructure, subject to the condition that, in the case of lifeline infrastructure that is a highway or bridge, the repair, reconstruction, restoration, retrofit, or replacement of that highway or bridge does not result in additional through travel lanes;

“(xi) notwithstanding any other provision of law, any proposed agency action associated with transmission activities described in section 216A(b) of the Federal Power Act;

[p. 20, line 4](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=20) (indent level 4)

“(xii) notwithstanding any other provision of law, any proposed agency action associated with a covered activity (as defined in subsection (i)(1) of section 7 of the Natural Gas Act (15 U.S.C. 717f));

“(xiii) a proposed agency action, the effects of which were previously evaluated by another agency in compliance with this Act; or

“(I) carried out under—

“(19) PROGRAMMATIC ENVIRONMENTAL DOCUMENT.— The term ‘programmatic environmental document’ means an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement analyzing all or some of the environmental effects of a policy, program, plan, or group of related actions.

[p. 21, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=21) (indent level 2)

“(20) PROJECT SPONSOR.—The term ‘project sponsor’ means an entity, including any Federal, private, public-private, State, local (including a county, borough, parish, city, and any other political subdivision of a State), or Tribal entity, that seeks an authorization for a proposed agency action.

[p. 21, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=21) (indent level 2)

- CEQ Chairman charged with standardizing procedures across agencies ([p. 26, line 2 to p. 26, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=26))

## Selected statutory quotes

[p. 25, line 17 to p. 25, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=25)

Agencies get 180 days to conform their procedures.

# Sec. 1105. Procedure for determination of level of review

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1105)

## Summary

Expands when an agency can skip an environmental document. An agency may apply one or a combination of categorical exclusions (but may not stack the same size-based exclusion repeatedly), may rely on a categorical exclusion Congress created, and may treat a state or tribal environmental review, or compliance with another federal law, as serving NEPA's function. A project sponsor can ask the lead agency to stop an environmental assessment and go straight to an environmental impact statement. If the lead agency decides no environmental document is needed, no other agency may prepare one.

## Key points

- Combination of multiple categorical exclusions allowed ([p. 28, line 8 to p. 28, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=28))
- State or tribal review that serves a similar function can substitute for federal review ([p. 29, line 1 to p. 29, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=29))
- Sponsor can demand an EIS instead of an EA ([p. 30, line 22 to p. 31, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=30))
- Lead agency threshold determination binds all other agencies ([p. 31, line 8 to p. 31, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=31))

## Selected statutory quotes

> If a lead agency determines that an environmental document is not required to be prepared with respect to a proposed agency action under subsection (a), no agency shall prepare an environmental document with respect to the proposed agency action.

[p. 31, line 5 to p. 31, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=31)

The lead agency's decision that no document is needed binds every other agency.

> the lead agency determines that the review serves a similar function as Federal agency compliance with this Act

[p. 29, line 1 to p. 29, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=29)

A state or tribal review can take the place of a federal one.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

NEPA section 106 (FRA 2023) already lets agencies apply their own or another agency's categorical exclusions; combining exclusions, statutory exclusions, state or tribal substitution and the binding threshold determination are new.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 did not amend NEPA section 106.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(b)) added the same two grounds for skipping a document (another statute or a state or tribal review that serves NEPA's function) and the same rule that a lead agency's threshold call binds other agencies. It also limited agencies to effects proximately caused by the project, which the Senate bill does not. Combining exclusions and the sponsor's right to request an EIS are Senate additions.

# Sec. 1106. Timely and unified Federal reviews

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1106)

## Summary

Rewrites NEPA section 107, the core of the review process. Environmental assessments are due in 1 year and environmental impact statements in 2 years, measured from the earlier of the agency's determination or its notice that the application is complete. A record of decision follows a final EIS within 45 days. Agencies in the review must decide all authorizations within 90 days, and agencies outside it within 120 days.

Lead agency designation gets a clock, with the CEQ Chairman resolving disputes within 21 days by a final, unreviewable decision. The Chairman can also order a resolution of interagency disputes, and that order counts as full compliance with any interagency consultation obligation under federal law.

The lead agency must drop any alternative that does not meet the purpose and need or the goals of a non-federal sponsor. Agencies need not consider science published after the notice of intent. Public scoping comment periods run 45 to 60 days, or 75 with the sponsor's consent.

If an agency defies a Chairman's dispute order and a deadline is missed, then after 30 days its permitting officers and senior executives must spend at least half their workweek on the overdue review. Once any deadline is 60 days overdue, the agency head may not travel more than 25 miles from the duty station until the document or permit issues. The Secretary of Defense is exempt. Project sponsors can sue over missed deadlines. The court must rule within 120 days and can order a decision within 60 days.

## Key points

- EIS in 2 years, EA in 1 year, with the clock starting at the earlier of the review determination or a complete application ([p. 46, line 17 to p. 46, line 18](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=46))
- ROD within 45 days of the final EIS; all federal permits within 90 days (120 for non-participating agencies) ([p. 49, line 8 to p. 49, line 11](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=49))
- No duty to consider scientific research published after the notice of intent ([p. 43, line 12 to p. 43, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=43))
- CEQ Chairman's dispute orders are final, unreviewable, and satisfy any interagency consultation requirement ([p. 52, line 11 to p. 52, line 13](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=52))
- Agency head confined to 25 miles of the duty station once a deadline is 60 days overdue; senior staff spend half the week on the review when the agency has defied a CEQ dispute order ([p. 53, line 13 to p. 53, line 17](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=53))
- Sponsors get a cause of action with a 120-day court decision clock ([p. 58, line 3 to p. 58, line 6](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=58))
- Alternatives that do not meet the non-federal sponsor's goals are eliminated ([p. 38, line 11 to p. 38, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=38))

Research published after the notice of intent need not be considered.

[p. 54, line 17 to p. 54, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=54)

The agency head's travel is restricted once a deadline is 60 days overdue.

> shall, for purposes of judicial review of the ultimate agency action and all other Federal law, constitute full compliance with and satisfaction of any requirement for interagency consultation, coordination, concurrence, authorization, or other procedural obligation under Federal law that is the subject of the dispute or delay.

[p. 52, line 14 to p. 52, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=52)

A CEQ dispute order satisfies consultation duties under other statutes.

> eliminate from consideration any alternative (except for a no-action alternative) that does not— “(I) fulfill the purpose and need of the proposed agency action; and “(II) meet the goals of an applicable non-Federal project sponsor.

[p. 38, line 6 to p. 38, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=38)

Alternatives that miss the sponsor's goals are dropped from the analysis.

> the lead agency shall publish an environmental impact statement, if applicable, not later than the date that is 2 years

[p. 48, line 17 to p. 48, line 20](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=48)

The two-year deadline for an environmental impact statement.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 set the 2-year EIS and 1-year EA deadlines, page limits of 150 pages for an EIS and 75 for an EA (both kept), and a sponsor's right to petition a court, which can order the agency to act within 90 days.

New here: the clock no longer starts at the notice of intent. A record of decision is due 45 days after the EIS and all permits within 90 or 120 days. Agencies need not consider science published after the notice of intent. The CEQ Chairman settles lead-agency and interagency disputes with final, unreviewable orders, and lead-agency disputes take 21 days, down from 40. Alternatives that miss the sponsor's goals are dropped. Missed deadlines can trigger the staff-time and travel sanctions, and courts must rule on deadline suits within 120 days.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 did not rewrite NEPA section 107; its deadlines were project-specific (energy leasing, rights-of-way).

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(c)) kept the 2023 deadlines and added a science cutoff at the earlier of the application or the notice of intent, a requirement that the purpose and need 'meet the goals of the applicant', 21-day clocks for cooperating agencies, and a final agency action within 30 days of the finished document. It had no CEQ dispute orders and no sanctions on agency staff or agency heads.

# Sec. 1107. Programmatic environmental document

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1107)

## Summary

Doubles the shelf life of programmatic environmental documents from 5 years to 10 years before an agency must reevaluate them.

## Key points

- Programmatic documents can be relied on for 10 years, up from 5 ([p. 62, line 1 to p. 62, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=62))

## Selected statutory quotes

> by striking “5 years” and inserting “10 years”.

[p. 62, line 1 to p. 62, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=62)

The whole section.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

FRA 2023 set 5 years.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(d)) made the same 5-to-10-year change and also let agencies rely on an earlier review for a substantially similar action; the Senate bill handles that through its exclusion for actions another agency already evaluated.

Section 108 of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4336b) is amended, in each of paragraphs (1) and (2), by striking “5 years” and inserting “10 years”.


# Sec. 1108. Use of categorical exclusions by other agencies

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1108)

## Summary

Requires every agency to report all its categorical exclusions to CEQ within 30 days and each new one within 7 days; CEQ keeps a public register on its website. An agency may adopt another agency's exclusion after consulting it and documenting the adoption.

## Key points

- Government-wide public register of categorical exclusions at CEQ ([p. 63, line 6 to p. 63, line 8](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=63))
- Streamlined adoption of other agencies' exclusions ([p. 63, line 16 to p. 63, line 19](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=63))

## Selected statutory quotes

> The Council shall maintain, on the website of the Council, an accurate and publicly available record of each categorical exclusion

[p. 63, line 6 to p. 63, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=63)

CEQ must keep a public list of every categorical exclusion.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

FRA 2023 section 109 already allows adoption of another agency's exclusion after consultation and public notice; the CEQ register and notification deadlines are new.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(e)) changed one phrase so agencies could adopt exclusions enacted by Congress. The CEQ register and the 30-day and 7-day reporting duties are Senate additions.

Extracted from the official PDF; line cites mark paragraph starts. Consult the PDF for exact layout.

[p. 62, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=62) (indent level 0)

# Sec. 1109. Applications for authorizations

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1109)

## Summary

Sets an application clock: within 60 days an agency must say whether an application is complete, and within another 60 days it must tell the sponsor whether the action is excluded from NEPA, needs an environmental assessment, or gets a notice of intent for an EIS. Applicants must submit a list of all known permits, a record of stakeholder engagement, and a statement of purpose and need.

## Key points

- 60 days to declare an application complete; 60 more to pick the level of review ([p. 65, line 14 to p. 65, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=65))
- Applicants file a record of stakeholder engagement with the application ([p. 67, line 1 to p. 67, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=67))

## Selected statutory quotes

> not later than 60 days after the date on which the project sponsor submits the application, the Federal agency shall— “(A) document receipt of the application; and “(B)(i) notify the project sponsor that the application is complete

[p. 64, line 22 to p. 65, line 4](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=64)

The 60-day completeness check.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

New. The current section 110 ordered CEQ to study a permitting portal; that study is replaced by the eNEPA mandate in section 1121.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(c)(4)) had the same 60-day completeness check and 60-day level-of-review decision. The required list of permits, record of stakeholder engagement and purpose-and-need description are Senate additions.

# Sec. 1110. Judicial review

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1110)

## Summary

Adds a judicial review section to NEPA. Suits challenging an authorization on NEPA grounds must be filed within 150 days. The party must allege an actual or imminent injury amounting to direct harm. Where a comment period was offered, the party must also have filed a sufficiently detailed comment. The federal court of appeals for the circuit where the project sits gets original and exclusive jurisdiction, with random judge assignment.

If a court finds a NEPA violation, the only remedy is remand without vacatur or injunction, with a fix deadline of no more than 180 days. The permit stays in effect and the project can proceed during the remand. A preliminary injunction is available only for a likely violation of a law other than NEPA or the National Historic Preservation Act.

Courts must give substantial deference to agencies on the scope and content of environmental documents. No NEPA suit may be brought over an action on tribal trust lands unless the tribe itself sues or effects reach beyond trust lands. No suit may rest on an omission from the sponsor's stakeholder engagement record.

## Key points

- 150-day statute of limitations ([p. 68, line 1 to p. 68, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=68))
- Only a party with a direct-harm injury can sue, and where a comment period was offered it must have commented ([p. 68, line 10 to p. 68, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=68))
- Court of appeals has original and exclusive jurisdiction ([p. 69, line 1 to p. 69, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=69))
- Remand without vacatur is the sole NEPA remedy; the project continues during the remand ([p. 69, line 24 to p. 70, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=69))
- No preliminary injunction for NEPA or NHPA violations alone ([p. 70, line 17 to p. 70, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=70))
- Substantial deference to agencies on the scope and contents of the document ([p. 73, line 25 to p. 74, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73))

## Selected statutory quotes

> the only remedy the court may order to redress that violation is to remand, without vacatur or issuance of an injunction, the applicable authorization to the agency

[p. 69, line 24 to p. 70, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=69)

Remand is the only remedy; a court cannot vacate or enjoin.

> a claim shall be barred unless the claim— “(1) is filed not later than 150 days

[p. 67, line 24 to p. 68, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=67)

The 150-day filing deadline.

> In reviewing a claim of whether an authorization complies with the requirements of this Act, a court shall afford substantial deference to the agency relating to the scope and contents of an environmental document.

[p. 73, line 23 to p. 74, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73)

Courts must defer to the agency on scope and contents.

> The activity that is the subject of an authorization remanded under paragraph (5)(A) may, notwithstanding that remand, be carried out

[p. 71, line 20 to p. 71, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=71)

The project can proceed during the remand.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

NEPA has no limitations period of its own, so the general 6-year limit on suits against the United States applies, with 2 years for FAST-41 covered projects and 150 days for highway and transit projects. There is no statutory prior-comment rule, cases start in district court, and courts can vacate or enjoin an approval.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 (sec. 101) set a 150-day limit for energy and mineral project authorizations and a 180-day remand deadline. It did not require prior comment, did not change standing, and left courts their ordinary remedies. That section survives as section 2201 of this bill.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 3) had the same core: 150 days, prior comment, direct harm, substantial deference, remand without vacatur or injunction, a 180-day fix deadline, and the tribal trust carve-out. Differences: the House bill barred challenges to the creation of categorical exclusions, required courts to rule within 180 days of receiving the record and appeals within another 180, and applied its remand rule to court orders entered before enactment. The Senate bill drops those three, moves cases to the courts of appeals with random assignment, lets construction continue during a remand in express terms, and allows a preliminary injunction when a different federal law is likely violated.

[p. 73, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73) (indent level 3)

“(B) EXCEPTIONS.—Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to an action for administrative or judicial review—

[p. 73, line 15](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73) (indent level 4)

“(i) brought by the Indian Tribe for which the United States holds the lands, minerals, or other resources in trust; or

[p. 73, line 18](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73) (indent level 4)

“(ii) that involves reasonably foreseeable effects of the final agency action that occur outside the lands, minerals, or other resources held in trust by the United States for the benefit of an Indian Tribe.

[p. 73, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=73) (indent level 1)

“(d) ROLE OF COURT.—In reviewing a claim of whether an authorization complies with the requirements of this Act, a court shall afford substantial deference to the agency relating to the scope and contents of an environmental document.

[p. 74, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=74) (indent level 1)

“(e) PROHIBITION ON CERTAIN CLAIMS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW.—Notwithstanding any other provision of law, there shall not be a claim or judicial review of whether a final agency action complies with the requirements of this Act for any omission from the list described in section 3(22)(B).

[p. 74, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=74) (indent level 1)

“(f) EFFECT.—Nothing in this section—

[p. 74, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=74) (indent level 2)

“(1) establishes a cause of action or a right to judicial review;

“(3) affects the right to obtain review under section 107(g)(4).”.


# Sec. 1121. Council on Environmental Quality

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1121)

## Summary

Replaces NEPA section 209 with an eNEPA technology mandate. Within 60 days CEQ must publish data standards for permitting data, within 120 days guidance on minimum functional requirements (automated project screening, case management, GIS tools, AI-assisted comment analysis, administrative-record tools), and agencies must begin implementing within 180 days. CEQ and the key permitting agencies build an ePermit unified interagency data system and a public authorization portal hosted by GSA. A pilot is due within a year and the system by December 1, 2028, 'to the maximum extent practicable'. Congress gets access to the AI prompts and fine-tuning data agencies use. CEQ also sets outcome-based performance measures for agencies and staff. Authorizes $5 million a year for NEPA.

## Key points

- Government-wide permitting data standards within 60 days ([p. 76, line 2 to p. 76, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=76))
- Public ePermit portal hosted by GSA, targeted for December 1, 2028 ([p. 92, line 18 to p. 92, line 21](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=92))
- AI-assisted comment analysis and screening tools named in statute; Congress gets the prompt configurations ([p. 90, line 22 to p. 91, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=90))
- Agency and personnel performance measures tied to the Permitting Improvement Fund ([p. 94, line 15 to p. 94, line 18](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=94))

## Selected statutory quotes

> Automated comment compilation and analysis tools, including services for comment categorization and response that handle the lifecycle of comment submission, analysis, categorization, and response with artificial intelligence support where appropriate.

[p. 80, line 1 to p. 80, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=80)

AI support for comment analysis is written into the statute.

> not later than December 1, 2028, the Chairman shall develop and implement the ePermit unified interagency data system

The target date for the ePermit system.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

The 2023 law ordered CEQ to study a permitting portal. This section orders one built.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The House passed a separate ePermit Act alongside the SPEED Act in December 2025 with similar goals; the SPEED Act itself did not include it.

## Summary

Definitions for the permitting tracker subtitle. A 'transparency project' is any action that needs an EIS, or an environmental assessment still unfinished 13 months past its deadline.

## Key points

- Every EIS project becomes a tracked transparency project ([p. 97, line 8 to p. 97, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=97))

## Selected statutory quotes

> a proposed agency action requiring the preparation of an environmental impact statement

[p. 97, line 8 to p. 97, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=97)

Every project with an impact statement goes on the tracker.

# Sec. 1132. Environmental Review and Permitting Tracker

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1132)

## Summary

Requires CEQ, with GSA, to run a public Environmental Review and Permitting Tracker listing every EIS project within 14 days of its notice of intent, with location, purpose and need, sponsor and agency contacts, quarterly schedule-compliance status explaining every slip and who caused it, and litigation status.

## Key points

- Public tracker for every EIS project ([p. 98, line 2 to p. 98, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=98))
- Each schedule change must say whether the agency or the sponsor caused it ([p. 100, line 7 to p. 100, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=100))

## Selected statutory quotes

> an explanation of each modification, including whether the modification is due to a delay on the part of an agency or the project sponsor

[p. 100, line 7 to p. 100, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=100)

The tracker must say whether the agency or the sponsor caused each delay.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

The federal Permitting Dashboard tracks FAST-41 covered projects. This tracker covers every project with an impact statement.

## Summary

Creates a Permitting Improvement Fund at Treasury that CEQ can transfer to permitting agencies for detailees, training, project managers, standardized processes, and public engagement. Authorizes $20 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2033.

## Key points

- $20 million a year, FY2027-2033, spent at CEQ's discretion ([p. 101, line 17 to p. 101, line 18](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101))

## Selected statutory quotes

[p. 102, line 14 to p. 102, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=102)

$20 million a year for the fund.

[p. 101, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 1)

(a) ESTABLISHMENT.—There is established in the Treasury of the United States a fund, to be known as the “Permitting Improvement Fund” (referred to in this section as the “Fund”).

[p. 101, line 11](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 1)

(b) PURPOSE.—The purpose of the Fund is to improve the performance of key permitting agencies with respect to timely environmental reviews and authorizations required under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.).

[p. 101, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 1)

(c) TRANSFER AUTHORITY.—Amounts in the Fund shall be available to the Chairman to transfer to a key permitting agency for 1 or more uses described in subsection (d).

[p. 101, line 20](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 1)

(d) USE OF AMOUNTS.—Amounts transferred under subsection (c) shall be used by a key permitting agency—

[p. 101, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 2)

(1) to support interagency detailee and rotation opportunities;

[p. 101, line 24](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=101) (indent level 2)

(2) to facilitate professional development;

[p. 102, line 1](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=102) (indent level 2)

(3) to enhance support for agency project managers;

## Summary

Requires EPA to use notice-and-comment rulemaking when it develops Clean Water Act water quality criteria, and routes challenges to those criteria and to any definition of 'waters of the United States' directly to the federal courts of appeals.

## Key points

- WOTUS definitions reviewed in courts of appeals, not district courts ([p. 103, line 7 to p. 103, line 9](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=103))
- Water quality criteria become rulemakings ([p. 102, line 23 to p. 102, line 25](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=102))

Challenges to a 'waters of the United States' definition go to the courts of appeals.

# Sec. 1202. Clean Water Act permitting and State certification

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1202)

## Summary

Rewrites Clean Water Act section 401 state certification. Certification is limited to water quality requirements. A state may deny only on clear and convincing evidence that no condition could make the project comply, and may impose only conditions that are necessary, least burdensome, and consistent with the federal permit.

The process gets a prefiling meeting, a defined complete application, a 3-day receipt acknowledgment, a 90-day completeness notice, and a review period of up to 1 year that can be extended only if the applicant asks in writing and the certifying authority agrees in writing. Silence is a waiver. Denials must name the specific water quality requirement violated. On judicial review the burden of proof falls on the state by clear and convincing evidence.

For interstate gas pipelines and bulk-power transmission lines, certification covers only direct point source discharges and must be decided within 9 months.

## Key points

- Certification scope narrowed to water quality requirements; clear-and-convincing standard for denials ([p. 104, line 19 to p. 104, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=104))
- One-year cap, extendable only at the applicant's written request and with the state's written agreement ([p. 115, line 22 to p. 115, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=115))
- Burden of proof on the state in court ([p. 117, line 5 to p. 117, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=117))
- Interstate pipelines and transmission lines: point-source discharges only, 9-month clock ([p. 121, line 15 to p. 121, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=121))

## Selected statutory quotes

> no certifying authority may— “(i) deny certification for any reason other than making a determination by clear and convincing evidence that no modification to or reasonable condition on the certification would make it possible to grant the certification without violating water quality requirements

[p. 104, line 24 to p. 105, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=104)

A state can deny only when no condition could make the project comply.

> a court shall place the burden of proof on the certifying authority to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that no reasonable modifications to or reasonable conditions on the certification would make it possible to grant the certification

[p. 117, line 5 to p. 117, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=117)

In court, the state carries the burden of proof.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

Section 401 lets states certify that a discharge complies with state water quality standards and 'any other appropriate requirement of State law', with a reasonable period not to exceed 1 year; EPA's 2020 and 2023 rules fought over the scope. The bill codifies a narrow scope similar to the 2020 rule, adds the clear-and-convincing standard and the point-source-only rule for pipelines and transmission.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024; Senate Republicans had sought section 401 limits in earlier bills such as Capito's 2023 RESTART Act.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

Not in the SPEED Act.

# Sec. 1204. Permits for dredged or fill material

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1204)

## Summary

Limits EPA's section 404(c) veto to the period between a complete application and permit issuance. Extends nationwide permits from 5 to 10 years, lets the Corps modify them mid-term, and requires it to keep nationwide permits 12, 14, 43, 57 and 58 for projects filling under 2 acres, which are deemed a minimal adverse effect. Reissuing a nationwide permit needs no Endangered Species Act consultation, only a programmatic environmental assessment under NEPA, and no National Historic Preservation Act consultation, so long as the permit does not loosen preconstruction requirements.

## Key points

- No section 404(c) veto before an application or after a permit issues ([p. 124, line 4 to p. 124, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=124))
- Nationwide permits last 10 years ([p. 125, line 2 to p. 125, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=125))
- Under 2 acres of fill is a minimal effect by statute ([p. 125, line 19 to p. 125, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=125))
- No ESA or NHPA consultation to reissue a nationwide permit that keeps its preconstruction requirements ([p. 128, line 7 to p. 128, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=128))

## Selected statutory quotes

> shall consider any effects of a discharge of dredged or fill material into less than 2 acres of navigable waters to be a minimal adverse environmental effect.

[p. 125, line 19 to p. 125, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=125)

Fills under 2 acres count as minimal by statute.

> no consultation with a Federal agency pursuant to section 7(a)(2) of that Act (16 U.S.C. 1536(a)(2)) is required

[p. 127, line 20 to p. 127, line 22](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=127)

Reissuing a nationwide permit needs no Endangered Species Act consultation.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

EPA may veto a disposal site at any time, including after a permit issues (Mingo Logan v. EPA, D.C. Circuit, 2013). Nationwide permits run 5 years. A 2020 district court ruling held that reissuing Nationwide Permit 12 required Endangered Species Act consultation.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

Not in the SPEED Act.

# Sec. 1205. Judicial review timeline clarity

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1205)

## Summary

Adds a 150-day statute of limitations for challenges to section 404 permits, general permits, verifications and state program approvals. Where a draft was published with at least 30 days for comment, a plaintiff must have commented on the issue. Remedies are limited to remand, with vacatur or injunction available only on a finding of imminent and substantial danger to health or the environment. Remand deadlines are capped at 180 days.

## Key points

- 150-day limit on 404 permit suits ([p. 129, line 21 to p. 129, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=129))
- Permits stay in force on remand absent imminent and substantial danger ([p. 132, line 9 to p. 132, line 13](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=132))

## Selected statutory quotes

# Sec. 1302. Timeline for Section 7 consultations

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1302)

## Summary

Shortens ESA section 7 formal consultation from 90 to 60 days, and the applicant-consent extension from 150 to 100 days. If consultation stretches past 145 days without the applicant's written consent, the applicant may sue under the APA for agency action unlawfully withheld. Consultation on any project with a NEPA document must finish by the NEPA deadline, unless the Secretary grants an extension for extraordinary circumstances.

## Key points

- Formal consultation: 60 days, not 90 ([p. 134, line 16 to p. 134, line 17](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=134))
- Consultation must end when the NEPA document is due, absent an extension for extraordinary circumstances ([p. 136, line 10 to p. 136, line 13](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=136))
- APA remedy after 145 days ([p. 135, line 23 to p. 135, line 24](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=135))

## Selected statutory quotes

> the consultation process under subsection (a)(2) shall be completed by not later than the date on which the applicable environmental document (as so defined) for the agency action is completed

[p. 136, line 4 to p. 136, line 8](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=136)

Consultation must end by the NEPA deadline.

# Sec. 1304. State assumption of consultation responsibilities

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1304)

## Summary

Creates ESA section 7A letting the Interior Secretary assign section 7 consultation duties to a state, by written agreement, for projects entirely inside the state. Interior must propose a rule within 270 days. States must show legal, financial and staffing capacity, waive sovereign immunity, accept federal court jurisdiction, keep public-records laws comparable to FOIA, and meet the same deadlines as the Secretary. Interior audits annually for 4 years, can terminate after a 120-day cure period, and applicants may still choose federal consultation. Interior's failure to act on an application within 180 days counts as a failure to act under the NEPA sanctions section.

## Key points

- States can take over ESA consultation, modeled on NEPA assignment for highways ([p. 137, line 25 to p. 138, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=137))
- Applicants can opt out and consult with the Interior Department instead ([p. 148, line 7 to p. 148, line 10](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=148))
- Annual audits for 4 years; 10-year renewable agreements ([p. 146, line 22 to p. 146, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=146))

## Selected statutory quotes

> the Secretary may assign, and the State may assume, the consultation responsibilities of the Secretary within the boundary of the State under subsections (a), (b), and (c) of section 7.

[p. 140, line 1 to p. 140, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=140)

The assignment of consultation to a state.

### Current law

No mechanism exists; consultation is federal-only (only the Fish and Wildlife Service and NMFS issue biological opinions).

# Sec. 1401. Maintaining Federal authorizations or permits for projects with non-Federal sponsors

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1401)

## Summary

For projects with non-federal sponsors, a federal agency may not revoke, suspend, amend, or otherwise interfere with a federal authorization in effect on or after September 16, 2026.

There are five exceptions. A court can order the action. The holder can have materially breached the permit or the law, or obtained the permit by fraud. The action can be needed to prevent specific, urgent, substantial and proximate harm to life, property, national security or defense, based on new information not considered in the original review. Or the holder can ask for it.

Agencies must give written notice with the statutory authority and evidence. The sponsor can sue in district court, where the agency carries the burden by clear and convincing evidence and classified information is reviewed in camera. A winning sponsor gets the permit reinstated, an injunction against repeat interference without a court order, attorney fees, delay costs, and an additional 25 to 50 percent of all project costs incurred, paid from the Judgment Fund without appropriation.

Where a stop-work order issued within the year before enactment was enjoined, the same judge keeps jurisdiction.

## Key points

- No permit revocation absent a court order, breach, fraud, new-information emergency, or the holder's request ([p. 159, line 20 to p. 159, line 21](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=159))
- Burden on the government by clear and convincing evidence ([p. 162, line 4 to p. 162, line 6](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=162))
- Damages of 25 to 50 percent of costs incurred, plus fees and delay costs, from the Judgment Fund ([p. 164, line 3 to p. 164, line 6](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=164))
- Where a stop-work order from the year before enactment was enjoined, the same judge hears any new attempt ([p. 165, line 1 to p. 165, line 3](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=165))
- Cutoff date of September 16, 2026 for permits in effect ([p. 159, line 14 to p. 159, line 15](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=159))

## Selected statutory quotes

> a Federal department or agency shall not take any new action that would revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter a Federal authorization or permit in effect on or after September 16, 2026

[p. 159, line 11 to p. 159, line 15](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=159)

The bar on revoking or altering an issued permit.

> costs in an amount equal to not less than 25 percent and not more than 50 percent of the total of all costs incurred by the non-Federal project sponsor or holder of the Federal authorization or permit in connection with the project

[p. 164, line 3 to p. 164, line 8](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=164)

A winning sponsor recovers 25 to 50 percent of project costs.

> If, within 1 year prior to the date of enactment of this Act, a Federal Agency has issued a stop-work order that would interfere with or prevent the construction or operation at full capacity of a project and said order has been enjoined by a court of competent jurisdiction

[p. 165, line 1 to p. 165, line 7](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=165)

A stop-work order enjoined in the year before enactment stays with the same judge.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

New. Agencies today can suspend or revoke leases and permits under each statute and the permit's own terms, subject to APA review with the burden on the challenger.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

Not in EPRA 2024; this title responds to 2025 and 2026 events.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

The SPEED Act (sec. 2(b)) had a shorter version of this rule inside NEPA: the same five exceptions, a clear-and-convincing standard 'as appropriate and where feasible', and APA review in the court of appeals. It had no damages and no cutoff date, and its section 4 exempted any agency action the administration had moved to reconsider since January 20, 2025, which covered the offshore wind approvals then under review. The Senate bill has no such exemption, covers permits in effect on or after September 16, 2026, shifts the burden of proof to the agency, adds money damages, and keeps the same judge on projects whose stop-work orders were already enjoined.

# Sec. 1402. Ensuring fairness for specific types of covered projects

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1402)

## Summary

Creates a cause of action for applicants in 46 named energy project types, plus any similar type a court certifies. The list runs from onshore and offshore wind, solar and storage to coal, gas, oil, nuclear, geothermal, transmission, pipelines, mining, hydrogen, hydropower, LNG and carbon storage.

The applicant must show a 'pattern of disparate treatment': an intentional, statistically demonstrated rise in denials or delays for that project type, compared with the prior 5 years. The pattern must last 180 days after enactment for permits without a NEPA document, or 280 days for those with one. Executive orders and official statements showing bias count as supporting evidence. The government must produce 5 years of raw statistics or face an adverse inference.

Permits for these projects that need no NEPA document must be decided within 1 year of a complete application.

Remedies are an injunction, fees, economic damages, and 50 to 100 percent of the expected construction cost, paid from the Judgment Fund. The applicant must finish the project or repay. Class actions are barred, and suits cannot be filed until 180 or 280 days after enactment.

## Key points

- Anti-discrimination rule across 46 named project types, from offshore wind to coal, plus any similar type a court certifies ([p. 172, line 13 to p. 172, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=172))
- Executive orders and officials' statements admissible as evidence of bias ([p. 176, line 11 to p. 176, line 17](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=176))
- Damages of 50 to 100 percent of expected construction cost ([p. 179, line 20 to p. 179, line 23](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=179))
- One-year deadline for permits that need no NEPA document ([p. 173, line 5 to p. 173, line 8](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=173))
- Claims mature 180 or 280 days after enactment ([p. 181, line 23 to p. 181, line 25](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=181))

# Sec. 1403. Avoiding unreasonable delays in permitting

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/1403)

## Summary

Gives applicants for permits that need no environmental document a right to sue in district court when the 1-year deadline in section 1402(c) is missed. The agency is excused if it proves the delay was caused by a disaster, a national emergency, fraud, withheld information, or a lapse in appropriations of more than 14 days. Courts decide within 120 days and can order a decision within 60 days.

## Key points

- Deadline suits for non-NEPA permits ([p. 183, line 3 to p. 183, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=183))

## Selected statutory quotes

> issue a decision under this section as expeditiously as practicable, but not later than 120 days, after the date on which the petition is filed

[p. 184, line 22 to p. 184, line 24](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=184)

The court must rule within 120 days.

# Sec. 2101. Transmission permitting

BAAJA draft released September 30, 2026. AI-assisted analysis; proposed changes.

Saved AI review: 401 supported, 12 flagged, 127 unchecked of 540 statements; checked 2026-10-01; stale: true. Coverage excludes current-law comparison cells and some research paraphrases. Read data/core.json checks for link and quote results and their dates. A stale review does not verify the current wording.

[Official PDF](https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf) · [Browser section](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/#/bill/sec/2101)

## Summary

Overhauls FERC's backstop siting authority under Federal Power Act section 216. FERC must issue a construction or modification permit for an interstate line of 230 kilovolts or more, or an advanced-conductor line at a voltage FERC sets, when it makes the required findings. The line no longer has to sit in a national interest corridor designated by the Energy Department. The state's clock for deciding now starts on the date the application is filed with the state.

FERC must find the line is in the public interest, protects or benefits consumers, and improves reliability. For lines of 345 kilovolts or more the developer may file at FERC at the same time as at the state. FERC must take landowner input, consider the state record, and give a 45-day comment period.

Costs go only to customers who benefit, in line with cost causation, and customers with no or trivial benefit cannot be charged involuntarily. Clean Water Act section 401 certifications and other state approvals under federal law become 'Federal authorizations' coordinated by FERC as lead agency (Interior for offshore), with challenges heard in the courts of appeals. ERCOT is excluded.

## Key points

- No more national interest corridor prerequisite for FERC backstop siting ([p. 199, line 15 to p. 199, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=199))
- The state's clock starts on the date the application is filed with the state ([p. 189, line 2 to p. 189, line 5](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=189))
- 230 kV threshold; simultaneous state and FERC filing at 345 kV and above ([p. 189, line 17 to p. 189, line 19](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=189))
- Cost allocation limited to beneficiaries; no involuntary charges for trivial benefits ([p. 194, line 13 to p. 194, line 14](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=194))
- State 401 certifications for transmission folded into FERC-led federal authorization schedule ([p. 195, line 10 to p. 195, line 12](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=195))
- ERCOT excluded; public power and small co-ops only if they opt in ([p. 198, line 24 to p. 199, line 2](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=198))

## Selected statutory quotes

> the Commission shall, after notice and an opportunity for hearing, including a public comment period of at least 45 days, issue one or more permits to individual or joint applicants for the construction or modification of electric transmission facilities necessary in the national interest

[p. 188, line 10 to p. 188, line 16](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=188)

FERC 'shall' issue the permit once it makes the findings.

> Customers that receive no benefit, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be allocated, from electric transmission facilities constructed or modified under this section shall not be involuntarily allocated any of the costs of those transmission facilities

[p. 194, line 9 to p. 194, line 14](https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/bill.pdf#page=194)

Customers with no or trivial benefit cannot be charged.

## Comparison notes

- [SPEED Act (H.R. 4776), engrossed in House](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr4776eh/html/BILLS-119hr4776eh.htm)
- [Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (S. 4753), reported in Senate](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s4753rs/html/BILLS-118s4753rs.htm)

### Current law

Section 216 (2005, amended 2021) says FERC 'may' site lines, and only inside National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors designated by the Energy Department. FERC can step in where a state lacks siting authority, has not decided within 1 year, has denied the application, or has set conditions that make the line uneconomic. Those grounds stay. The cost allocation and lead-agency changes are new.

### EPRA 2024 (reported S. 4753)

EPRA 2024 (sec. 401) made the same core change: FERC backstop siting without corridor designation, FERC action once a state has had 1 year, beneficiary-pays cost allocation and the trivial-benefit protection.

Differences: EPRA said FERC 'may' issue a permit after a 60-day comment period and set the floor at 100 kilovolts. This bill says 'shall' after 45 days and sets the floor at 230 kilovolts. It drops EPRA's findings that a line 'significantly reduce transmission congestion' and be 'consistent with sound national energy policy'. It adds simultaneous state and FERC filing at 345 kilovolts, the state record, an opt-in for public power and small co-ops, FERC-led coordination of state water certifications, and review of all related permits in the courts of appeals.

### SPEED Act (House-passed H.R. 4776)

Not in the SPEED Act, which amended only NEPA.
